entries.name: Chernozem
entries.weathers_to: luvisol with leaching; deep humus profile resists loss
entries.notes: The black earth of Ukraine and the Great Plains: near-black, 10x richer in humus than average soil, 1-2 m deep. Among the most productive farmland on Earth.

entries.name: Alluvium
entries.notes: River-borne silt deposited on floodplains: Nile, Ganges, Yangtze. Fresh, deep and fertile; the reason all great grain civilizations started on rivers.

entries.name: Loess
entries.notes: Wind-blown glacial silt; Chinese Loess Plateau runs up to ~300 m thick. Stands in vertical cliffs, erodes in torrents when wet.

entries.name: Quartz sand
entries.notes: Desert dunes and beaches; Namib dunes run deeper than 100 m. Loose grains, no cohesion: flows and shifts, never holds a wall.

entries.name: Podzol
entries.weathers_to: spodic horizon deepens; quartz parent material remains
entries.notes: The ash-grey Russian podzol: a bleached white E horizon under raw conifer litter. Poor farmland, good timber land.

entries.name: Cambisol (brown earth)
entries.notes: The default good brown soil of temperate Europe: weathered subsoil without much clay migration. Workhorse of mixed-forest farming.

entries.name: Laterite (Oxisol)
entries.notes: Deep, iron-rich tropical weathering; cuts soft when dug, hardens in air. Angkor's temples are laterite. Profiles can reach tens of metres.

entries.name: Ultisol (red-yellow podzolic)
entries.notes: The red clay of the US Piedmont and southeast China: leached, acidic, low in plant nutrients. Grows pine well; needs lime and fertiliser for crops.

entries.name: Aridisol
entries.notes: Pale, weakly developed desert soil; almost no leaching, so salt and carbonate build up in the profile instead of washing away.

entries.name: Kastanozem (chestnut soil)
entries.notes: Chernozem's drier cousin: Alberta prairies, Kazakh steppe. Less humus, still fertile with enough rain.

entries.name: Luvisol (grey brown earth)
entries.notes: Clay washes out of the topsoil and packs into a dense Bt horizon below. Widespread across temperate Europe and northern China.

entries.name: Terra rossa
entries.notes: Brick-red clay filling fissures in limestone karst; nearly everything soluble has washed out, iron oxide remains. Famed for Croatian and Italian wine country.

entries.name: Rendzina (Rendzic Leptosol)
entries.type: thin dark soil on limestone or chalk
entries.notes: Often under 25 cm deep on chalk and limestone. Champagne's vineyards grow on chalk rendzina. Dark, sticky, full of shell fragments.

entries.name: Andosol (volcanic ash soil)
entries.notes: Black, fluffy, and impossibly fertile; bulk density often under 0.9. Feeds Java, Japan and the Andes; Mount St. Helens ash (1980) still warms local yields.

entries.name: Vertisol (black cotton soil)
entries.weathers_to: persists; churns itself by shrinking and swelling
entries.notes: Cracks open in the dry season and swells shut when wet; the only soil that ploughs itself. India's black cotton soil is the classic example.

entries.name: Permafrost (Gelisol)
entries.weathers_to: thermokarst ponds and gleyic soils when it thaws
entries.notes: Ground frozen for two or more years; up to ~1,500 m thick in Yakutia, over 700 m across much of the Arctic. Only the 0.2-2 m active layer thaws each summer.

entries.name: Histosol (peat)
entries.notes: Bog-grown, water-logged organic matter; some peatlands are 10-20 m deep. Preserves corpses, pollen and trackways for millennia.

entries.name: Gleysol
entries.notes: Blue-grey with mottled rust where air sneaks in: the colour of iron with no oxygen. Marks a marsh or poor drainage more surely than any map.

entries.name: Kaolin (china clay)
entries.notes: Weathered-out feldspar turned white and pure; Cornwall and Georgia supply the world's porcelain and coated paper.

entries.name: Bentonite
entries.notes: Swells to many times its dry volume when wet; named for Fort Benton, Wyoming. The universal gap-filler of geology and industry.

entries.name: Caliche (calcrete)
entries.weathers_to: dissolves in humid climates; persists in dry ones
entries.notes: Rain pulls carbonate down and evaporation cements it into a stone layer 1-5 m down. Enough to stop a pickaxe and a plough share alike.

entries.name: Silcrete
entries.notes: Opaline silica welding sand and rubble into near-quartzite. Tougher than the bedrock it caps; classic Aboriginal tool stone of the Australian interior.

entries.name: Bauxite
entries.notes: What laterite becomes when everything washable has washed away: the world's aluminium. Guinea and Australia hold the biggest deposits.

entries.name: Marl
entries.notes: Halfway between limestone and clay; soft enough to crumble in the hand. Romans burned marl for cement; farmers still spread it to fix sour soil.

entries.name: Solonchak
entries.notes: White salt crust over salty mud: Aral Sea basin and coastal playas. Upped groundwater evaporates and leaves the pan white.

entries.name: Solonetz
entries.notes: The black alkali soil: columnar clay breaks that split into pillar-like peds. Barren or sour enough that only alkali-tolerant plants grow.

entries.name: Sierozem (grey desert soil)
entries.notes: The pale grey-fawn soil of Central Asia's deserts: weakly developed, carbonate-rich, salt-tolerant shrubs only. Oasis farms wring cotton and melons from it.

entries.name: Grus (rotten granite)
entries.notes: Granite weathered in place into grit, corestones and all: dig into a granite tor and the rock simply pours out as coarse sand.

entries.name: Terra preta (Amazonian dark earth)
entries.weathers_to: persists; charcoal resists decay for centuries
entries.notes: Pre-Columbian Amazonian kitchen middens, ~500 BCE-1500 CE; still regenerates its fertility today. The one soil humans built that outlasted its makers.

entries.name: Paddy soil (wet rice anthrosol)
entries.notes: Clay puddled to a waterproof pan and flooded; 2,000+ years of Asian rice culture turned marshes into the most productive farmland per hectare on Earth.

entries.name: Pozzolana
entries.notes: Ash from the Phlegraean Fields near Pozzuoli; mixed with lime it sets hard even underwater. The Pantheon and Roman harbour moles still stand on it.

entries.name: Fuller's earth
entries.notes: Named for the fullers who kneaded wool in it; English Surrey and Georgia supplied it for centuries. Drinks oil and grease greedily, and never gives it back.

entries.name: Sabkha (salt crust)
entries.weathers_to: gypsum crust, then dolomitic crust (interior playas)
entries.notes: The crust over coastal and interior salt pans of the Gulf and North Africa: blindingly white, knife-hard on top, wet brine mud inches below.

entries.name: Gypsum dune sand
entries.weathers_to: dissolves in wet climates; dunes migrate only in the dry
entries.notes: White Sands, New Mexico: the largest gypsum dune field on Earth, flaked from an ancient shallow sea. The dunes glisten like snow and stay cool.

entries.name: Quicksand
entries.notes: Ordinary sand turned fluid by upward water flow; cannot pull you under (you float), but cannot let go either. A hazard, not a building material.
